extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated writers interested in style and judging literature
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing 'easy' poetry and for judging works of art and literature; covers diction, ornament, the limits of rules, and the habits of good critics/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy poetry — natural diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy poetry is that in which natural thoughts are expressed without violence to the language. The discriminating character of ease consists principally in the diction; for all true poetry requires that the sentiments be natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid harsh or daring figures, transposition, unusual acceptations of words, and any licence which would be avoided by a writer of prose. Any artifice in construction removes ease. The effect of ease is that lines are expressed naturally; pleasure in reading secures attention and retention. Examples: the critic cites Pope's Iliad first lines as distorted by inversions and superfluities that abolish ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbal artifice and superfluity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any artifice appears in the construction of the verse, that verse is no longer easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific anti-patterns: inversions, epithets inserted only to lengthen the line, curious iteration of the same word, unusual though grammatical structures, harsh metaphors, and words used in uncommon senses. These practices produce obscurity and ruggedness and destroy the grace of easy poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake affectation for ease
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation, however opposite to ease, is sometimes mistaken for it; those who aspire to gentle elegance may adopt fashionable barbarisms and think this is ease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'female phrases' and modish locutions or fashionable barbarisms: stylistic fashions die with their inventors and so are not true ease. Easy style should be enduring and natural, not a current of ephemeral affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease can coexist with sublimity and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Ease, though it excludes pomp, will admit greatness; nor is ease more contrary to wit than to sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume simplicity precludes grandeur or wit. Examples cited: lines from Cato and Cowley show easy poetry can be sublime or witty. However, sustained easy sublimity over many lines is difficult and requires greater care than producing ornamented lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules cannot fully capture genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever part of an art can be executed or criticised by rules, that part is no longer the work of genius, which implies excellence out of the reach of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about over-reliance on formal rules when judging great works: servile attention to minute exactness may be inconsistent with higher excellency. Rules may help technical judgement but cannot account for the sublime elements of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism by parts is insufficient for whole works
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics who judge only by parts, reaching only inferior beauties, cannot determine the merit of extensive works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations that attend only to individual features (e.g., necks, hands, single devices) miss the unified effect and higher excellences of a work. Avoid letting partial rules dominate assessment of large-scale artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good criticism relies on immediate perception
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound critic often gives judgment from immediate perception rather than by mechanically applying lists of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception and direct responsiveness to a work often produce better judgment than learned talk enabled by memorized rules. Excessive rule-application can deprive the critic of the pleasure of the arts and blunt acute discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connoisseurship can be shallow and performative
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming the character of a connoisseur (name-dropping artists/terms and citing academy rules) may be a cheaper route than genuine critical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of the 'cant of criticism' — voluble assertion of names and principles without attached ideas. Example: a visitor applies modern 'rules' anachronistically to Raffaelle, criticizing qualities that would have been blemishes in that artist's higher class. Connoisseurship can create the appearance of judgement without substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match stylistic devices to genre and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality that is an excellence in a lower class may be a blemish in a higher; stylistic devices must suit the genre and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: quick, sprightly turns suit epigrams but would ill suit the majesty of heroic poetry. Evaluate whether particular techniques (harmony, affectation, light-and-shadow metaphors in painting; sprightliness in poetry) are appropriate to the intended dignity and scale of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art of memory is the art of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The true art of memory is the art of attention: no man will read with much advantage who cannot, at pleasure, evacuate his mind and bring to his author an intellect defecated and pure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To retain and learn material, the reader/writer must clear distracting cares and pleasures; what is read with delight is commonly retained because pleasure secures attention. Regular, deliberate renovation (repetition) helps retention. This has implications for writers: concentrated attention yields better assimilation and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive marginalia and mechanical transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: Noting everything in the margins or transcribing large quotations to a commonplace-book consumes time without reliably assisting memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hand has no closer correspondence with the memory than the eye; writing itself distracts thought, and reading twice is commonly better remembered than transcription. Don't substitute mechanical copying for attentive reading and mental renovation.
